sections.skill: Identify risk management strategies and explain how insurance transfers financial risk

questions.prompt: Luis pays a company $40 a month so that if his phone is stolen, the company pays for a replacement. Which risk strategy is this?

choices.text: Avoiding the risk by never owning a phone at all
Transferring the risk
Reducing the risk by using a stronger case
Keeping the risk and paying for losses himself

questions.intro: Four ways to manage risk: avoid it (do not do the risky thing), reduce it (make a loss less likely or smaller), retain it (pay for losses yourself), or transfer it (pay someone else, usually an insurer, to take the loss). Insurance is risk transfer.
questions.feedback: Insurance moves the cost of a loss to the insurer in exchange for a premium.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance

misconceptions.A: Avoiding means not doing the risky thing
misconceptions.C: Reducing lowers the chance or size of a loss

sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: In insurance, what does the word "premium" mean?

choices.text: The money the insurer pays after a covered loss
The part of a loss the policyholder pays first
A bonus paid to drivers with no accidents
The price paid for coverage

questions.intro: Key terms: the premium is what you pay for coverage (monthly or yearly). A claim is your request for payment after a loss. The deductible is the part of a covered loss you pay before the insurer pays.
questions.feedback: The premium is the cost of the policy.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance

misconceptions.A: Confuses premium with a claim payment

sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: A covered loss costs $3,000. Luis's deductible is $500. How much does the insurer pay?
questions.intro: For most property losses, the policyholder pays the deductible and the insurer pays the rest, up to the policy limit.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: How can insurers afford to pay large losses?

choices.text: The government refunds every claim the insurer pays
Insurers only sell to people who never have losses
Many people's premiums pool together
Policyholders repay the claim later with interest

questions.intro: Insurance pools risk: many people each pay a small, predictable premium, and the pool pays the few who have large losses.
questions.feedback: Pooling many premiums covers the few large losses.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: Which loss is most sensible to retain (pay yourself) rather than insure?

choices.text: A house fire that destroys everything you own
A crash that injures another driver badly
A long illness with large hospital bills
A $15 phone charger that breaks

questions.intro: Insurance matters most for losses that are unlikely but too large to afford. Small, affordable losses are often cheaper to retain, especially with an emergency fund.
questions.feedback: Retain small losses; insure the ones that could be financially devastating.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

sections.relationship: Insurance decisions compare how likely a loss is with how large it would be.

questions.prompt: Which word describes a chance of losing money or something of value?

choices.text: Equity
Risk
Liquidity
Principal

questions.feedback: Risk is the chance of loss.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: Wearing a seat belt is which risk strategy?

choices.text: Reducing the risk
Transferring the risk to another person
Avoiding the risk entirely
Retaining the risk on purpose

questions.intro: Reducing risk makes a loss less likely or less severe, such as seat belts, smoke alarms, or locks.
questions.feedback: Seat belts make injuries less severe: risk reduction.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance

misconceptions.B: No one else takes the loss
misconceptions.C: You still ride in the car
misconceptions.D: You are actively making the loss smaller

sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: Why does an emergency fund help with risk?

choices.text: It replaces the need for any insurance at all
It lowers the chance an accident happens
It covers small losses and deductibles
It earns enough to pay any lawsuit

questions.correct_answer: It covers small losses and deductibles
questions.feedback: Cash on hand lets you retain small losses and pay deductibles.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance

misconceptions.B: Money does not change the odds

questions.prompt: A renters policy has a $20,000 limit for personal property. A fire destroys $26,000 of belongings, and the deductible is $500. How much does the insurer pay?
questions.intro: A policy limit is the most an insurer will pay for a covered loss. The deductible is subtracted from the loss first; the insurer then pays the result, but never more than the limit.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance

misconceptions.D: Ignores the limit and the deductible
misconceptions.A: Subtracts the deductible from the limit

sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: A policy lists "Exclusions: flood, earthquake." What does that mean?

choices.text: Those losses are not covered
Those losses are covered with no deductible
Those losses are covered only on weekends
Those losses are paid at double the limit

questions.intro: Exclusions list what a policy does not cover. Flood insurance, for example, is usually a separate policy.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: What is the declarations page of a policy?

choices.text: A letter saying a claim was denied
A form to cancel the policy
A list of every claim you have filed
A summary of coverage, limits, and premium

questions.correct_answer: A summary of coverage, limits, and premium
questions.intro: The declarations ("dec") page shows who and what is covered, the limits, deductibles, and the premium.
questions.feedback: The dec page summarizes the policy.
questions.topic: Risk and the purpose of insurance
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: Replacement cost coverage pays to buy a new item; actual cash value pays the item's value minus depreciation. A 4-year-old TV cost $800 and is now worth $300. Under actual cash value, before any deductible, what is paid?
questions.intro: Replacement cost policies cost more but pay enough to replace items new.
questions.feedback: Actual cash value pays the depreciated value, $300.

questions.prompt: After a covered loss, what is a sound first step in filing a claim?

choices.text: Throw away damaged items before anyone sees them
Wait a year to see if more damage appears
Document the damage with photos
Exaggerate the loss to cover the deductible

questions.intro: Contact the insurer promptly, take photos, keep receipts, and prevent further damage.
questions.feedback: Photos and receipts support a claim.
